full_judgment:
3. We have perused the order dated 22-9-86 by which order, the learned Magistrate took cognizance against the petitioner and others of an offence punishable under section 188 of the Penal Code. In the said order, the learned Magistrate pointed out that in a proceeding under section 133 CrPC being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.26 of 1983, petitioner and others, MI6 were second party of the said proceedings were directed to remove obstructions from a river. The said order has been affirmed by the learned Sessions Judge. Thereafter, the learned Magistrate served a notice upon the petitioner and others on 15-7-85 to remove the obstruction by 20-7-435 but they did not remove the obstruction. Accordingly the learned Magistrate removed the obstruction with the help of police force on 11-7-85. Thereafter, the learned Magistrate sun moo drew up proceeding under section 188 Penal Code holding that petitioner and others disobeyed the order promulgated by public servant lawfully empowered to promulgate such order. The learned Magistrate was of the opinion that petitioner and others gave importance to their interest than that of court's order and thereby they have committed an offence under section 188 of the Penal Code. 

 4. Now the question is whether the learned Magistrate can suo moto initiate a proceeding under section 188 of the Penal Code without making a formal complaint for alleged disobedience of the order of Magistrate. Section 195(1)(a) provides that no court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under sections 172 to 188 of the Penal Code except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of some other public servant to whom he is subordinate. Upon perusal of the order of learned Magistrate, it appears that petitioner along with others have allegedly disobeyed the order of the then Upazila Magistrate and the Upazila Magistrate himself drew-up the proceeding against them. It further appears that the learned Magistrate without making a formal complaint by himself or of some other public servant to whom he is subordinate, took cognizance of offence by recording an order that the petitioner and others despite service of notice for removal of the obstruction, disobeyed the direction and thereby they have violated the order of the public servant. Such initiation of proceeding is contrary to sections 195(1) (a) CrPC. There is an embargo to initiate a proceeding that no court shall take cognizance of any offence punishable under section 172 to 188 of the Penal Code except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned. In the instant case, the learned Magistrate himself is the public servant whose order has been alleged to have been disobeyed by accused and therefore it was obligatory on the part of the learned Magistrate to make a written complaint alleging the nature of the order made by him which was alleged to have been disobeyed by accused and the manner of violation in order to form an opinion that accused persons have committed an offence punishable under section 188 of the penal Code. He can also direct his Subordinate Magistrate, if any to make a complaint. In this case the learned Magistrate did not follow the procedures provided in sections, 195(1) (a) CrPC and therefore, we are of the opinion that there is illegality in initiating the proceeding against petitioner and others. 

 5. Petitioner being aggrieved by the said order moved the learned sessions Judge in a revisional application under section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure being Criminal Motion No. 35 of 1998. The learned Sessions Judge though found that the learned Magistrate has committed illegality in drawing up proceeding without making a formal complaint, but rejected the Criminal Motion by judgment and order dated 28-5-95 holding that revisional application under section 438 of the Code is legally not maintainable after the Sessions Judges have been invested with the powers under section 4313A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Sessions Judge was totally confused of the scope and application of section 438 of the Code Even after the amendment of the Code of Criminal Procedure by Ordinance No. XLIX of 1978 empowering Sessions Judges to exercise revisional powers under section 439A all or any of the powers which may be exercised by the High Court Division under section 349 of the said Code, the powers of the Sessions Judge to report to the High Court Division with a recommendation for orders as to the regularity of any proceedings of any inferior court have not been altered but kept alive. In Pakistan Sessions Judges have been given revisional powers under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure by Law Reforms Ordinance 1972 enabling them to exercise all or any of the powers conferred on High Court by section 439 in cases relating to proceedings before Magistrates subordinate to itself. There was corresponding amendment to section 438 whereby words "The Sessions Judge" have been deleted. After such amendment, section 438 stands, as follows: 

 In India as per recommendation of the Law Commission in its 41st report sessions Judges have been given the power to finally dispose of revision taken up by themselves under section 399 of the Code and the order of the Sessions Judge has been given finality. By the said amendment, the powers of the Sessions Judges or District Magistrate to report with a recommendation of orders to the High Court have been deleted but similar provisions as provided in section 438(2) of our Code have been kept in section 400 enabling Additional Sessions Judge to exercise jurisdiction only in respect of cases transferred to them which reads: 

 "400 Power of Additional Sessions Judge—An Additional Sessions Judge shall have and may exercise all powers of Sessions Judge under this chapter in respect of any case which may be transferred to him by or under any general or special order of the Sessions Judge." 

 6. In a comparison of the provision of the Code empowering Sessions Judges to exercise revisional powers, in Pakistan and India it appears to us that in India and Pakistan, Sessions Judges have been given revisional powers to make final orders but at the same time, their powers under section 438 to recommend to the High Court for orders have been taken away. In Bangladesh sessions Judges have been given revisional powers to make final orders but simultaneously their powers to make recommendation to the High Court Division for orders under section 438 which they had before amendment have been kept intact, Therefore, the intention of the legislature is clear and obvious. It is that a litigant has been given option to choose the forum, whether he would avail the powers of the Sessions Judge either under section 438 or under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. When a litigant resorts to section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, Sessions Judges must read section 435 of the said Code together, because section 438 is not independent of section 435. In other words section 438 should be read along with and subject to the provisions of section 435. Sections 435 and 438 prescribe the method by which records of any criminal case comes to the High Court Division and the power of the High Court Division to deal with the record. 

 7. Even on an application moved under section 438 before the Sessions Judges, they can exercise powers under section 439A and can make final orders in a given case. This powers of making final order upon as application moved under section 438, in our opinion, should not be invoked and/or be made against the person who is the petitioner before them because there is finality of the order in respect of him. If a litigant who moves the Sessions Judge under section 439 A, or if the Sessions Judge makes a final order, the decision of the Sessions Judge thereon in relation to the petitioner is final in view of sub-section (2) of section 439A. The petitioner before the Sessions Judges, even if he is aggrieved by such decision is deferred from moving the High Court Division under Section 439. Sub-section (4) of section 439 completely bars the High Court Division to entertain an application against another passed by Sessions Judge under section 439A. Therefore, we are of the opinion that the legislature has consciously kept section 438 alive, even the Sessions Judges have been invested with the powers under section 439A. to make final orders enabling the litigants to choose the forum as to whether he would resort to the forum provided under section 438 or under section 439A with the risk of finality of the order that may be passed in relation to him only. Therefore, the learned Sessions Judge erred in law in presuming that the revisional application was not maintainable. 

 9. Proceedings in Criminal Case No.116 of 1986 pending in the Court of Upazila Magistrate, Jagannathpur, District Sunamganj are quashed.
